claim: Genes positioned in the 5' portion of both HoxA (Hoxa7 to Hoxa13) and HoxD (Hoxd8 to Hoxd13) clusters were expressed at all developmental stages (E12.5, E16.5, and E18.5) in the genital tubercle.
source: We observed that genes positioned in the 5' portion of both HoxA (Hoxa7 to Hoxa13) and HoxD (Hoxd8 to Hoxd13) clusters were expressed at all developmental stages (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: With the exception of Hoxc11 and Hoxc10, only basal levels of mRNAs were scored for the HoxC and HoxB clusters in the genital tubercle.
source: Furthermore, with the exception of Hoxc11 and Hoxc10, only basal levels of mRNAs were scored for the HoxC and HoxB clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1), consistent with previous observations (Hostikka and Capecchi, 1998; Montavon et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and consistent with previous published observations.

claim: A general decrease in the amount of Hox mRNAs was detected during GT development, in particular for Hoxd12 and Hoxd13.
source: Overall, we detected a general decrease in the amount of Hox mRNAs during GT development, in particular for Hoxd12 and Hoxd13 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hoxd13 transcripts were detected in the cloaca region at E10.5.
source: We performed RT-qPCR for Hoxd13 and detected transcripts in the CR at E10.5 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a significant increase in Hoxd13 transcript levels between the cloaca region at E10.5 and the E12.5 GT (p<0.0001).
source: followed by a significant increase in transcript levels between the CR and the E12.5 GT (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: Hoxd13 mRNA levels remained constant between E12.5 and E13.5 GT.
source: The mRNA levels then remained constant between E12.5 and E13.5
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Hoxd13 transcript levels were significantly reduced in the interval between E13.5 and E15.5 GTs (p<0.0001).
source: whereas they were significantly reduced in the interval between E13.5 and E15.5 GTs (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: After E15.5, Hoxd13 transcript levels continued to decrease to a lesser extent (between E15.5 and E18.5; p=0.0175).
source: After E15.5, the transcript levels continued to decrease yet to a lesser extent (between E15.5 and E18.5; p=0.0175, Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: At E10.5, prior to GT formation, all Hoxd genes and Evx2 were accessible as defined by ATAC-seq.
source: At E10.5, prior to GT formation, all Hoxd genes and Evx2 were accessible as defined by ATAC-seq (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: H3K27ac signals of moderate intensity were scored over the Hoxd9 to Evx2 DNA interval as well as peaks over the promoters of Hoxd1, Hoxd3, and Hoxd4 at E10.5.
source: H3K27ac signals of moderate intensity were scored over the Hoxd9 to Evx2 DNA interval as well as peaks over the promoters of Hoxd1, Hoxd3, and Hoxd4 (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: H3K27me3 marks were detected mostly over the Evx2 gene, next to the Hox cluster at E10.5.
source: This was confirmed by a low coverage in H3K27me3 marks, which were detected mostly over the Evx2 gene, next to the Hox cluster (Figure 1C, gray area).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the growing E13.5 genital bud, a whole inactivation of the cluster from Hoxd1 to Hoxd10-11 was observed, as indicated by robust coverage of this region by H3K27me3 marks and the disappearance of both H3K27ac marks and ATAC-seq signals.
source: In the growing E13.5 genital bud, a different picture was observed with a whole inactivation of the cluster from Hoxd1 to Hoxd10-11, as indicated by a robust coverage of this region by H3K27me3 marks and the disappearance of both H3K27ac marks and ATAC-seq signals (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks remained in the Hoxd11 to Evx2 region at E13.5, accompanied by a large increase in H3K27ac signals.
source: In contrast, ATAC-seq peaks remained in the Hoxd11 to Evx2 region, accompanied by a large increase in H3K27ac signals (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At E13.5, a clear separation of the cluster into two distinct epigenetic domains was scored, reminiscent of the situation described in distal forelimb buds.
source: At this stage, a clear separation of the cluster into two distinct epigenetic domains was scored, reminiscent of the situation described in distal forelimb buds (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data, and compared to previous published observations.

claim: At E17.5, the dichotomy between epigenetic domains, as labelled by the H3K27ac and ATAC-seq signals, was still detected though at a lower magnitude.
source: At E17.5, this clear dichotomy between epigenetic domains, as labelled by the H3K27ac and ATAC-seq signals, was still detected though at a lower magnitude (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: H3K27me3 marks started to spread over the entire gene cluster at E17.5.
source: In parallel, H3K27me3 marks started to spread over the entire gene cluster (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Hoxd genes are regulated in the developing GT by long-range acting sequences positioned within the flanking centromericly located TAD (C-DOM).
source: Hoxd genes are regulated in the developing GT by long-range acting sequences positioned within the flanking centromericly located TAD (C-DOM; Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on previous studies and supported by 4C-seq data.

claim: Hoxd13 was selected as a viewpoint for 4C-seq since it is the highest expressed Hoxd gene in the genital tubercle and is necessary for proper genital development.
source: Hoxd13 was selected as a viewpoint since it is the highest expressed Hoxd gene in this tissue and because it is necessary for proper genital development.
evidence: Based on expression data and previous functional studies.

claim: The disruption of Hoxd13 alone leads to alterations in external genitals.
source: Indeed, while its disruption alone leads to alterations in external genitals, its combined inactivation with Hoxa13 leads to a complete agenesis of genitals (Dollé et al., 1993; Kondo et al., 1997; Warot et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The combined inactivation of Hoxd13 with Hoxa13 leads to a complete agenesis of genitals.
source: Indeed, while its disruption alone leads to alterations in external genitals, its combined inactivation with Hoxa13 leads to a complete agenesis of genitals (Dollé et al., 1993; Kondo et al., 1997; Warot et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mESC, contacts between Hoxd13 and the C-DOM were mainly scored in the island II and V regions.
source: In mESC, contacts between Hoxd13 and the C-DOM were mainly scored in the island II and V regions (Figure 2B, top, red lines).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In mESC, a large proportion of the interactions was scored in the cluster itself where they were likely driven by H3K27me3 marks.
source: A large proportion of the interactions was scored in the cluster itself where they were likely driven by H3K27me3 marks (Vieux-Rochas et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data and previous published observations.

claim: The 3D architecture in mESC was altogether quite comparable to that found in forebrain cells.
source: This 3D architecture was altogether quite comparable to that found in forebrain cells, with discrete contacts established between Hoxd13 and island II and V (Figure 2B, bottom, red lines)
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The 4C-seq profiles in mESC and forebrain cells reflected the 3D chromatin state of C-DOM in the complete absence of transcription.
source: and hence we estimate that these profiles reflected the 3D chromatin state of C-DOM in the complete absence of transcription.
evidence: Based on inference from 4C-seq data comparing transcriptionally inactive tissues.

claim: Upon transcriptional activation, frequencies of contacts with the C-DOM increased and interactions between Hoxd13 and previously characterized enhancers (Prox, GT2) became visible.
source: Upon transcriptional activation, however, frequencies of contacts with the C-DOM increased and interactions between Hoxd13 and previously characterized enhancers (Prox, GT2) (Gonzalez et al., 2007; Lonfat et al., 2014) became visible (Figure 2B, second track, blue lines).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2B and previous characterization of enhancers.

claim: The E10.5 CR dataset showed a C-DOM specific chromatin architecture that is organized before the emergence of the genital bud.
source: This dataset showed a C-DOM specific chromatin architecture that is organized before the emergence of the genital bud.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data from E10.5 CR.

claim: In subsequent stages of GT development (E12.5 or E13.5), contacts between various enhancer regions and Hoxd13 continued to increase when compared to the CR sample.
source: In subsequent stages of GT development (E12.5 or E13.5), contacts between various enhancer regions and Hoxd13 continued to increase when compared to the CR sample (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: As development further progressed, contacts established between Hoxd13 and C-DOM weakened.
source: As development further progressed, contacts established between Hoxd13 and C-DOM weakened.
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data.

claim: At later stages, the 4C-seq profile observed was comparable to either forebrain cells or the mESC profiles, with a loss of contacts with specific enhancers (Prox and GT2).
source: At the latter stage the profile observed was comparable to either forebrain cells or the mESC profiles, with a loss of contacts with specific enhancers (Prox and GT2; Figure 2B, blue lines).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The relative frequency of contacts with island II and island V remained fairly constant in all samples analyzed.
source: The relative frequency of contacts with island II and island V remained fairly constant in all samples analyzed.
evidence: Supported by quantification of 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The contacts between Hoxd13 and either Prox or GT2 dramatically increased from the mESC to the E13.5 GT samples.
source: In contrast, the contacts between Hoxd13 and either Prox or GT2 dramatically increased from the mESC to the E13.5 GT samples.
evidence: Supported by quantification of 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The decrease in contacts observed between E13.5 to E17.5 GTs correlated with a decrease in Hoxd13 transcript levels.
source: The decrease in contacts observed between E13.5 to E17.5 GTs correlated with a decrease in Hoxd13 transcript levels.
evidence: Based on correlation between 4C-seq and transcript level data.

claim: Fetal forebrain cells, which do not express any Hoxd genes, showed the lowest values of interactions between Hoxd13 and either Prox or GT2.
source: Fetal forebrain cells, which do not express any Hoxd genes, showed the lowest values of interactions between Hoxd13 and either Prox or GT2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The interactions between GT2 and the Hoxd13 region substantially decreased from E13.5 to E17.5.
source: We confirmed that the interactions between GT2 and the Hoxd13 region substantially decreased from E13.5 to E17.5
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data using GT2 as viewpoint shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Contact frequencies between island V and Hoxd13 was essentially stable, regardless of the stage and tissue analyzed.
source: whereas contact frequencies between island V and Hoxd13 was essentially stable, regardless of the stage and tissue analyzed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data using island V as viewpoint shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: As transcription decreased, some contacts established with C-DOM were lost whereas others were maintained (island II and island V).
source: Therefore, as transcription decreased, some contacts established with C-DOM were lost whereas others were maintained (island II and island V)
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data analysis.

claim: At the time transcription is switched off, C-DOM goes back to the pre-organized chromatin backbone that characterizes tissues or cells that do not express any Hox genes.
source: indicating that at the time transcription is switched off, C-DOM goes back to the pre-organized chromatin backbone that characterizes tissues or cells that do not express any Hox genes.
evidence: Based on inference from 4C-seq data comparing different developmental stages.

claim: The constitutively contacted island V includes a binding site occupied by CTCF.
source: Of note, the constitutively contacted island V includes a binding site occupied by CTCF (see below), a protein described to facilitate enhancer-promoter contacts by DNA-looping (see Ong and Corces, 2014)
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data and previous literature.

claim: CTCF is a protein described to facilitate enhancer-promoter contacts by DNA-looping.
source: Of note, the constitutively contacted island V includes a binding site occupied by CTCF (see below), a protein described to facilitate enhancer-promoter contacts by DNA-looping (see Ong and Corces, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CTCF does not always appear necessary in the process of facilitating enhancer-promoter contacts.
source: even though it does not always appear necessary in this process (Bonev et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2012; Stadhouders et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A detailed analysis of CR ATAC-seq dataset revealed several accessible chromatin sites, some of which match previously identified GT enhancers such as GT2.
source: A detailed analysis of our CR ATAC-seq dataset revealed several accessible chromatin sites, some of which match previously identified GT enhancers such as GT2 (Lonfat et al., 2014; Figure 3A, black arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3A and previous enhancer characterization.

claim: The GT and limb enhancer sequence Prox was not yet accessible at E10.5 CR stage.
source: Noteworthy, the GT and limb enhancer sequence Prox was not yet accessible at this stage (Figure 3A, red arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At E13.5, when the C-DOM is fully active, several ATAC-seq peaks were scored over previously characterized enhancers within this region, including Prox and GT2.
source: At E13.5, when the C-DOM is fully active, several ATAC-seq peaks were scored over previously characterized enhancers within this region, including Prox and GT2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In E17.5 GT, as development progressed, ATAC-seq peaks were lost in the C-DOM correlating with the decrease in both Hoxd transcript levels and chromatin interactions.
source: In E17.5 GT, as development progressed, these peaks were lost in the C-DOM (Figure 3A, arrows) correlating with the decrease in both Hoxd transcript levels and chromatin interactions (see above).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3A and correlation with previous data.

claim: In the Del(rel1-rel5) allele, a 47% reduction in Hoxd13 mRNA levels was scored in the GT (p=0.0005).
source: In these mutant mice, a 47% reduction in Hoxd13 mRNA levels was scored in the GT (p=0.0005)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: In the Del(rel1-rel5) allele, Hoxd12, Hoxd11 and Hoxd10 were less affected than Hoxd13.
source: whereas Hoxd12, Hoxd11 and Hoxd10 were less affected (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mice carrying the Del(rel5-SB) deletion displayed a 76% reduction in Hoxd13 mRNA levels (p<0.0001).
source: Mice carrying this deletion displayed a greater effect on the steady-state level Hoxd13 mRNAs, which was reduced by 76% (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: In the Del(rel5-SB) allele, Hoxd12, Hoxd11 and Hoxd10 were affected to a lower extent than Hoxd13.
source: Again, Hoxd12, Hoxd11 and Hoxd10 were affected to a lower extent (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Del(IV-SB) allele showed a 38% decrease in the amount of Hoxd13 mRNAs (p=0.0066).
source: We next analyzed the Del(IV-SB) allele and noticed a 38% decrease in the amount of Hoxd13 mRNAs (p=0.0066)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: In the Del(IV-SB) allele, no significant effect was detected for Hoxd12, Hoxd11, or Hoxd10.
source: yet no significant effect was detected for any other genes (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: In the Del(SB-Atf2) allele, a slight but significant upregulation of Hoxd13 mRNA levels (p=0.003) was observed in the GT.
source: Finally, we looked at the Del(SB-Atf2) allele where the most centromeric part of the TAD had been deleted. In these mutant mice, we observed a slight but significant upregulation of Hoxd13 mRNA levels (p=0.003) in the GT
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis.

claim: In the Del(SB-Atf2) allele, Hoxd12, Hoxd11, and Hoxd10 were not affected.
source: whereas other genes were not affected (Figure 3E and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Several non-overlapping regions located within C-DOM are required for the transcriptional activation of Hoxd13 in the developing GT.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that several non-overlapping regions located within C-DOM are required for the transcriptional activation of Hoxd13 in the developing GT.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple deletion experiments.

claim: The Prox enhancer accounted for the majority of chromatin interactions with Hoxd13 in the region between the rel1 and rel5 breakpoints.
source: In this genomic interval the limb- and GT-specific Prox enhancer (Figure 4B) accounted for the majority of chromatin interactions with Hoxd13
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data.

claim: The Prox enhancer was accessible in the GT at E13.5 as seen by ATAC-seq.
source: and was accessible in the GT at E13.5 as seen by ATAC-seq (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Del(Prox) allele showed a 36% decrease in the expression of Hoxd13 by RT-qPCR in E12.5 GTs (p=0.006).
source: We generated the Del(Prox) allele, a 13 kb large deletion including the Prox sequence (Figure 4A), and observed a 36% decrease in the expression of Hoxd13 by RT-qPCR in E12.5 GTs (p=0.006) (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis.

claim: The severe impact of Del(Prox) on Hoxd13 expression seemed to be exclusively quantitative, as the Hoxd13 expression pattern detected by whole mount in situ hybridization remained spatially unchanged.
source: This severe impact seemed to be exclusively quantitative, as the Hoxd13 expression pattern detected by whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) remained spatially unchanged (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Prox enhancer accounts for more than a third of the Hoxd13 transcriptional efficiency and is thus a major contributor to this regulation in GT.
source: This result indicated that the Prox enhancer accounts for more than a third of the Hoxd13 transcriptional efficiency and is thus a major contributor to this regulation in GT.
evidence: Based on inference from RT-qPCR data showing 36% decrease.

claim: The ATAC-seq profiles revealed no obvious change in chromatin accessibility throughout the C-DOM after the deletion of Prox.
source: The ATAC-seq profiles revealed no obvious change in chromatin accessibility throughout the C-DOM after the deletion of Prox (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When examining the potential importance of Prox in building the C-DOM interaction landscape by 4C-seq using Hoxd13 as a viewpoint, only minor alterations in the frequency of contacts between Hoxd13 and discrete cis-regulatory elements were noticed.
source: Likewise, when we examined the potential importance of Prox in building the C-DOM interaction landscape by 4C-seq using Hoxd13 as a viewpoint, we noticed only minor alterations in the frequency of contacts between Hoxd13 and discrete cis-regulatory elements (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The Prox enhancer, while of critical importance for regulating Hoxd13, does not actively contribute to the general architectural organization of the locus.
source: We thus concluded that the Prox enhancer, while of critical importance for regulating Hoxd13, does not actively contribute to the general architectural organization of the locus.
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq and 4C-seq data showing no major architectural changes.

claim: The genomic interval positioned between the SB and the rel5 breakpoints accounted for 76% of Hoxd13 expression in the incipient genital bud.
source: We next focused on the genomic interval positioned between the SB and the rel5 breakpoints (Figure 5A), since this region accounted for 76% of Hoxd13 expression in the incipient genital bud (see Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data from Del(rel5-SB) allele shown in Figure 3C.

claim: X-gal staining of E13.5 transgenic embryos revealed enhancer activity in the GT for the IIIE and IVE sequences.
source: X-gal staining of E13.5 transgenic embryos revealed enhancer activity in the GT for the IIIE and IVE sequences (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by transgenic assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The IIIE and IVE sequences showed complementary specificities, with IIIE active in dorsal GT cells, whereas the IVE sequence strongly labelled the ventral half of the GT.
source: in cellular territories included within the wider expression domain of Hoxd13 in this structure. These two sequences showed complementary specificities, with IIIE active in dorsal GT cells, whereas the IVE sequence strongly labelled the ventral half of the GT (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by transgenic assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Embryos injected with the E1 sequence showed a weak signal on the GT.
source: Embryos injected with the E1 sequence showed a weak signal on the GT (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by transgenic assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No staining was scored when using the VE or the E2 sequences in transgenic assays.
source: and no staining was scored either when using the VE, or the E2 sequences (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by transgenic assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The VE region includes a CTCF binding site and this particular sequence is the only strongly occupied CTCF site present in the ca. 550 kb large region between Evx2 and island II.
source: Of particular interest, the VE region includes a CTCF binding site and this particular sequence is the only strongly occupied CTCF site present in the ca. 550 kb large region between Evx2 and island II.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Out of the five regions tested, only E1, IIIE, and IVE showed some activity in the developing GT.
source: Therefore, out of the five regions tested, only E1, IIIE, and IVE showed some activity in the developing GT.
evidence: Based on transgenic assay results.

claim: The GT2 sequence showed a strong staining throughout the bud in transgenic embryos.
source: We also re-investigated the activity of the GT2 sequence in transgenic embryos and scored a strong staining throughout the bud (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by transgenic assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Individual enhancer elements within C-DOM display distinct and complementary patterns of activity (e.g., IIIE and IVE), while others show largely overlapping domains of expression (e.g., GT2).
source: These experiments highlighted the regulatory complexity of the C-DOM, with individual enhancer elements displaying distinct and complementary patterns of activity (e.g., IIIE and IVE), while others show largely overlapping domains of expression (e.g., GT2).
evidence: Based on inference from transgenic assay results.

claim: No significant difference was detected in Hoxd13 transcript levels or spatial patterns in any of the Del(GT2), Del(IV), Del(IIIE), Del(V) and Inv(V) alleles.
source: Unexpectedly, we did not detect any significant difference, either in transcript levels or in their spatial patterns, in any of the Del(GT2), Del(IV), Del(IIIE), Del(V) and Inv(V) alleles (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and WISH data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Unlike the Prox sequence, the GT2, IV, IIIE, and V sequences are not in themselves functionally important enough to elicit a visible transcriptional effect upon the main target gene, at least in the GT and at the developmental stage considered.
source: Unlike the Prox sequence analyzed above, these results suggest that none of these sequences is in itself functionally important enough to elicit a visible transcriptional effect upon the main target gene, at least in the GT and at the developmental stage considered.
evidence: Based on inference from deletion experiments showing no effect.

claim: Except for the loss of a single accessibility peak located between GT2 and CsB, the distribution of accessible DNA sequences over C-DOM appeared to be independent from the GT2 element.
source: Except for the loss of a single accessibility peak located between GT2 and CsB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, black arrows), the distribution of accessible DNA sequences over C-DOM appeared to be independent from the GT2 element (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The absence of global impact of the GT2 deletion was confirmed when using a viewpoint on Hoxd13 to evaluate by 4C-seq, potential reallocations of contacts in the mutant allele.
source: This absence of global impact of the GT2 deletion was confirmed when using a viewpoint on Hoxd13 to evaluate by 4C-seq, potential reallocations of contacts in the mutant allele.
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No salient change in the chromatin organization of C-DOM was observed after deletion of GT2.
source: There again, no salient change in the chromatin organization of C-DOM was observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), further indicating that the deletion of GT2 in isolation had essentially no effect on the global architecture of the C-DOM landscape.
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The GT2 enhancer is already accessible at E10.5 CR stage.
source: To explore this possibility, we used RT-qPCR to measure the Hoxd13 mRNA level in the CR at E10.5, a developmental stage where this enhancer is already accessible, as concluded from our ATAC-seq dataset (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, black arrow)
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At E10.5 CR stage, a slight (27%), but significant (p=0.0152) decrease in the expression of Hoxd13 was observed in Del(GT2) mutants.
source: At this early stage, we observed a slight (27%), but significant (p=0.0152) decrease in the expression of Hoxd13 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Figure 6—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: GT2 on its own may have a role in controlling Hoxd13 expression prior to GT formation.
source: suggesting that GT2 on its own may have a role in controlling Hoxd13 expression prior to GT formation.
evidence: Based on inference from RT-qPCR data showing decreased expression at E10.5 CR.

claim: Island V was shown to interact with Hoxd13 in all tissues and developmental stages analyzed.
source: Amongst the various sequences isolated in C-DOM, island V was shown to interact with Hoxd13 in all tissues and developmental stages analyzed thus far.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data from multiple stages and tissues.

claim: ChIP-seq results showed several CTCF binding sites in the centromeric part of C-DOM, primarily between island II and Atf2 and matching with other islands and 4C-seq peaks, close to the centromeric TAD boundary.
source: In the wildtype locus, our ChIP-seq results showed several CTCF binding sites in the centromeric part of C-DOM, primarily between island II and Atf2 and matching with other islands and 4C-seq peaks, close to the centromeric TAD boundary (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Island V was the only region between Evx2 and island II (approximately 550 kb) where a clear binding of CTCF was detected.
source: Of note, island V was the only region between Evx2 and island II (approximately 550 kb) where a clear binding of this protein was detected (Figure 7A, arrow).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A close examination of island V revealed a major CTCF binding site oriented towards the cluster and a weaker site observed nearby.
source: A close examination of this element revealed a major CTCF binding site oriented towards the cluster and a weaker site observed nearby.
evidence: Based on detailed analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: In the HoxD cluster, the distribution of bound CTCF was similar to that observed in limb buds cells, with a series of strong sites at its 5' extremity flanking Hoxd13 and orientated towards C-DOM.
source: In the HoxD cluster, the distribution of bound CTCF was similar to that observed in limb buds cells (Rodríguez-Carballo et al., 2017; Soshnikova et al., 2010), with a series of strong sites at its 5' extremity flanking Hoxd13 and orientated towards C-DOM (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The Del(V) allele showed a loss of the associated CTCF binding at island V.
source: As expected, the Del(V) allele showed a loss of the associated CTCF binding (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Strong CTCF binding to the major peak was detected in the Inv(V) allele in GT at E13.5, indicating that the inversion did not affect its binding capacity.
source: In contrast, strong CTCF binding to the major peak was detected in the Inv(V) allele in GT at E13.5, indicating that the inversion did not affect its binding capacity (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by CUT and RUN data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In mutant Del(V) GT cells, with the exception of the deleted region, no change in the ATAC-seq profile was observed when compared to control GT cells.
source: In mutant Del(V) GT cells, with the exception of the deleted region, we did not observe any change in the ATAC-seq profile (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) when compared to control GT cells.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the mutant Inv(V) GT cells, the loss of one ATAC-seq peak located between the GT2 and CsB sequences was observed.
source: In the mutant Inv(V) GT cells, we observed the loss of one ATAC-seq peak located between the GT2 and CsB sequences (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, black arrow)
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neither the deletion nor the inversion of the centrally-located CTCF site had any substantial effect on the accessibility of the remaining regulatory elements.
source: Therefore, neither the deletion nor the inversion of this centrally-located CTCF site had any substantial effect on the accessibility of the remaining regulatory elements
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: When Hoxd13 was taken as a viewpoint for the Del(V) allele, the global interaction profile between Hoxd13 and C-DOM was virtually identical to control.
source: When Hoxd13 was taken as a viewpoint for the Del(V) allele, the global interaction profile between Hoxd13 and C-DOM was virtually identical to control (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Using a viewpoint positioned on island IV, only a slight reduction in the frequency of contacts between island IV and Hoxd13 was scored in Del(V) allele.
source: We confirmed this result by using a viewpoint positioned on island IV, located nearby island V. Only a slight reduction in the frequency of contacts between island IV and Hoxd13 was scored (Figure 7B, black arrow).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Island V and its associated CTCF site seem to have a marginal importance in maintaining the global chromatin structure of this regulatory landscape.
source: Therefore, island V and its associated CTCF site seem to have a marginal importance in maintaining the global chromatin structure of this regulatory landscape.
evidence: Based on inference from 4C-seq data showing minimal changes.

claim: The majority of CTCF mediated chromatin loops are established between sites displaying opposite and convergent orientations.
source: The majority of CTCF mediated chromatin loops are established between sites displaying opposite and convergent orientations (i.e. with CTCF motifs pointing toward each other) (de Wit et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Qualitative analysis of the interaction profile generated using Hoxd13 as a viewpoint in Inv(V) allele revealed a slight disruption in the contacts between Hoxd13 and island V.
source: Qualitative analysis of the interaction profile generated using Hoxd13 as a viewpoint revealed a slight disruption in the contacts between Hoxd13 and island V (Figure 7C, red arrow).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Using a viewpoint on island V in Inv(V) allele, a reduction in the overall frequency of interactions in the region between island V and Hoxd13 was observed.
source: We validated this result by doing the reverse experiment and using a viewpoint on island V. In this set up, we observed a reduction in the overall frequency of interactions in the region between island V and Hoxd13 thus confirming the previous result (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In Inv(V) allele, an increase in the interaction frequency was observed in the region centromeric to island V up to island II and island C, that is with the next CTCF sites displaying opposite and convergent orientations in the mutant configuration.
source: Noteworthy, we observed an increase in the interaction frequency in the region centromeric to island V up to island II and island C, that is with the next CTCF sites displaying opposite and convergent orientations in the mutant configuration (Figure 7C, middle and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The inversion in the general tropism of interactions in Inv(V) allele supports the importance of CTCF site orientations in the loop-extrusion model.
source: This inversion in the general tropism of interactions supports the importance of CTCF site orientations in the loop-extrusion model (de Wit et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from 4C-seq data and comparison to loop-extrusion model.

claim: When island IV was used as a viewpoint in Inv(V) allele, a reduction in contacts with Hoxd13 was observed.
source: When we used island IV as a viewpoint, we also observed a reduction in contacts with Hoxd13 (Figure 7C, black arrow).
evidence: Supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Either the loss or the inversion of island V and its associated CTCF site had an effect on C-DOM chromatin structure, but this effect did not greatly alter the regulatory landscape chromatin architecture.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that either the loss or the inversion of island V and its associated CTCF site, had an effect on C-DOM chromatin structure. Nonetheless, this effect did not greatly alter the regulatory landscape chromatin architecture, corroborating the lack of impact on transcription.
evidence: Based on inference from 4C-seq data and correlation with transcription data.

claim: The same C-DOM TAD was previously shown to regulate Hoxd13 and neighboring Hoxd genes during distal limb bud development.
source: The same C-DOM TAD was previously shown to regulate Hoxd13 and neighboring Hoxd genes during distal limb bud development, a structure that resembles in many respects the developing genitals (Cobb and Duboule, 2005; Cohn, 2011; Infante et al., 2015; Tschopp et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The products of both Hoxa13 and Hoxd13 were shown to bind to most of those C-DOM regulatory sequences specific for distal limb buds.
source: In this case, the products of both Hoxa13 and Hoxd13 were shown to bind to most of those C-DOM regulatory sequences specific for distal limb buds.
evidence: Based on previous studies.

claim: HOX13 proteins themselves were instrumental in activating or re-enforcing transcription of the Hoxd13 gene in distal limb buds, by accumulating at this landscape and binding to many accessible sites due to their low binding specificity.
source: From this observation, it was concluded that HOX13 proteins themselves were instrumental in activating or re-enforcing transcription of the Hoxd13 gene in this developmental context, by accumulating at this landscape and binding to many accessible sites due to their low binding specificity (Beccari et al., 2016; Sheth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous work has shown both redundancy of binding to limb regulatory elements and similarity of DNA binding motifs between HOXA13 and HOXD13.
source: Previous work has shown both redundancy of binding to limb regulatory elements and similarity of DNA binding motifs between HOXA13 and HOXD13 (Sheth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Enrichment of HOX13 binding signals was detected in both HoxD regulatory landscapes (C-DOM and T-DOM) similar to what was observed in distal forelimb.
source: We detected enrichment of HOX13 binding signals in both HoxD regulatory landscapes (Figure 8A; C-DOM and T-DOM) similar to what was observed in distal forelimb (Beccari et al., 2016; Sheth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by CUT and RUN data shown in Figure 8A and comparison to previous studies.

claim: In CR cells at E10.5, HOX13 binding was found in C-DOM at discrete positions corresponding to previously described regulatory elements, in particular GT1, GT2, and Prox.
source: In CR cells at E10.5, HOX13 binding was found in C-DOM at discrete positions corresponding to previously described regulatory elements, in particular GT1, GT2, and Prox (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by CUT and RUN data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All HOX13 binding sites at E10.5 CR, with the exception of the Prox enhancer, correlated with accessible chromatin sites as mapped by ATAC-seq.
source: All these binding sites and others, with the exception of the Prox enhancer, correlated with accessible chromatin sites as mapped by ATAC-seq (Figure 8B, arrow).
evidence: Supported by comparison of CUT and RUN and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the case of Prox, HOX13 binding was scored before a clear ATAC-seq signal was detected, suggesting a potential role for HOX13 proteins in participating to making some of these sites accessible.
source: In the case of Prox, HOX13 binding was scored before a clear ATAC-seq signal was detected, suggesting a potential role for HOX13 proteins in participating to making some of these sites accessible.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of CUT and RUN and ATAC-seq data.

claim: The few strong ATAC-seq peaks at E10.5 CR, which were not matched by HOX13 binding, corresponded to non-Hox gene promoters.
source: The few strong ATAC-seq peaks, which were not matched by HOX13 binding corresponded to non-Hox gene promoters (Figure 8B, bottom line).
evidence: Based on analysis of ATAC-seq and CUT and RUN data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In E13.5 GT cells, as development progressed in parallel with C-DOM becoming fully active, an overall increase of HOX13 binding was scored over C-DOM.
source: In E13.5 GT cells, as development progressed in parallel with C-DOM becoming fully active, an overall increase of HOX13 binding was scored over C-DOM (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by CUT and RUN data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: While HOX13 binding was strengthened at some sites bound at the earlier stage, other elements became both accessible and bound by HOX13 such as the islands II and III regions or a sequence located inside an intron of the Lnpk gene.
source: While binding was strengthened at some sites bound at the earlier stage, other elements became both accessible and bound by HOX13 such as the islands II and III regions or a sequence located inside an intron of the Lnpk gene (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of CUT and RUN and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A good correlation was observed between the increase of Hoxd13 transcript levels on the one hand, and both the activation of the C-DOM regulatory landscape and the binding of HOX13, on the other.
source: Overall, a good correlation was observed between the increase of Hoxd13 transcript levels on the one hand, and both the activation of the C-DOM regulatory landscape and the binding of HOX13, on the other.
evidence: Based on correlation between transcript levels, ATAC-seq, and CUT and RUN data.

claim: In mammals, external genitals appear during fetal development as an overgrowth of a mesodermal territory surrounding the cloaca region.
source: In mammals, external genitals appear during fetal development as an overgrowth of a mesodermal territory surrounding the cloaca region (Georgas et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In the absence of both Hoxa13 and Hoxd13 functions, the growth of external genitals does not occur and the fetus displays a structure resembling that of a cloaca.
source: In the absence of both Hoxa13 and Hoxd13 functions, this growth does not occur and the fetus displays a structure resembling that of a cloaca (Kondo et al., 1997; Warot et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The proper transcriptional activation of Hoxa13 and Hoxd13 in time and space is critical for external genital development.
source: indicating that the proper transcriptional activation of these two genes in time and space is critical in this context.
evidence: Based on inference from previous studies showing phenotypes.

claim: The regulation of Hoxd13 is primarily achieved by the C-DOM TAD, a large regulatory landscape flanking the gene cluster on its centromeric side, which also controls Hoxd gene activation in the developing digits.
source: Studies of the HoxD cluster have provided some insights into this question (Lonfat et al., 2014) and suggested that the regulation of Hoxd13 is primarily achieved by the C-DOM TAD, a large regulatory landscape flanking the gene cluster on its centromeric side, which also controls Hoxd gene activation in the developing digits.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In developing digits, the chromatin interaction profile displayed some differences in transcriptionally active cells, even though the global TAD structure remained unchanged, suggesting that a C-DOM internal chromatin micro-organization had occurred due to the implementation of various digit-specific enhancers.
source: In the latter case, the chromatin interaction profile displayed some differences in transcriptionally active cells, even though the global TAD structure remained unchanged, suggesting that a C-DOM internal chromatin micro-organization had occurred due to the implementation of various digit-specific enhancers.
evidence: Based on previous observations and inference.

claim: Two types of chromatin interactions were observed at the Hoxd locus: contacts associated with a pre-formed structure, mainly linked to occupied CTCF sites, and interactions present only when transcriptional activation had occurred.
source: We looked at chromatin dynamics at the Hoxd locus and observed two types of chromatin interactions. On the one hand, we detected contacts associated with a pre-formed structure, mainly linked to occupied CTCF sites. These contacts were observed independently of the transcriptional status of the cluster, as exemplified by island II and island V. On the other hand, we scored interactions present only when transcriptional activation had occurred such as the Prox and GT2 enhancer sequences.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data analysis.

claim: The C-DOM TAD seems to be activated in a coordinated manner, with all specific contacts appearing mostly within the same developmental time window, suggesting that the TAD itself may be considered as a global regulatory unit.
source: Our time-point series of interaction profiles revealed that the C-DOM TAD seems to be activated in a coordinated manner, with all specific contacts appearing mostly within the same developmental time window, suggesting that the TAD itself may be considered as a global regulatory unit (see below), rather than a field containing a range of disparate enhancers with specific features and acting at different times.
evidence: Based on inference from time-series 4C-seq data.

claim: The chromatin architecture associated with the specific developmental context of GT was already observed in the E10.5 CR, that is before the emergence of the GT.
source: Also, the chromatin architecture associated with this specific developmental context was already observed in the E10.5 CR, that is before the emergence of the GT.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data from E10.5 CR.

claim: The internal-TAD micro-organization predates the outgrowth of the GT structure, which suggests a causal relationship or at least a necessity for the TAD to be fully primed for the structure to develop.
source: Therefore, this internal-TAD micro-organization predates the outgrowth of the GT structure, which suggests -but does not demonstrate- a causal relationship or at least a necessity for the TAD to be fully primed for the structure to develop.
evidence: Based on inference from temporal analysis of chromatin architecture, but noted as speculative.

claim: The highest frequency of interactions with C-DOM was scored in E12.5 and E13.5 GTs, which correlated with an increase in Hoxd13 transcription, an enrichment of H3K27ac marks and increase in binding of HOX13 proteins at discrete enhancer elements.
source: The highest frequency of interactions with C-DOM was scored in E12.5 and E13.5 GTs, which correlated with an increase in Hoxd13 transcription, an enrichment of H3K27ac marks and increase in binding of HOX13 proteins at discrete enhancer elements.
evidence: Based on correlation of 4C-seq, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT and RUN data.

claim: After E13.5, a decrease in Hoxd transcript levels was scored in parallel with a reduction of all contacts associated with the active regulatory regions within the C-DOM.
source: After this time-point, a decrease in Hoxd transcript levels were scored in parallel with a reduction of all contacts associated with the active regulatory regions within the C-DOM.
evidence: Based on correlation of RNA-seq and 4C-seq data.

claim: By E17.5 the C-DOM structure within the GT was reduced to a framework of constitutive interactions associated with CTCF binding sites, similar to the one observed in ES cells and fetal forebrain cells.
source: By E17.5 the C-DOM structure within the GT was reduced to a framework of constitutive interactions associated with CTCF binding sites, similar to the one observed in ES cells and fetal forebrain cells.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data analysis.

claim: The global decrease in Hoxd13 expression observed at a cell population level can be explained through the selective transcriptional switch-off in some cell types along with their progressive differentiation thus leading to a dilution effect.
source: This global decrease, observed at a cell population level, can be explained either through a general decrease in transcription or through the selective transcriptional switch-off in some cell types along with their progressive differentiation thus leading to a dilution effect. Detailed ISH analyses see Figures 2 and 3 in Dollé et al. (1991a) and Figure 1 in Warot et al. (1997) clearly favors the latter option
evidence: Based on inference from previous ISH analyses.

claim: At E17.5, strong Hoxd13 expression was scored in the anlagen of the corpus cavernosum while other cells of the tubercle became negative.
source: At E17.5 indeed, strong Hoxd13 expression was scored in the anlagen of the corpus cavernosum while other cells of the tubercle became negative.
evidence: Based on previous ISH analyses.

claim: The concentration of Hoxd13-positive cells in the blastema and subsequent restriction to the periphery resembles the situation for Hoxd13 transcripts during cartilage differentiation in developing digits.
source: Of note, this concentration of positive cells in the blastema and subsequent restriction to the periphery (Dollé et al., 1991a) resembles the situation for Hoxd13 transcripts during cartilage differentiation in developing digits.
evidence: Based on comparison to previous observations.

claim: A penile bone (baculum) differentiates from the corpus cavernosum region in the mouse as in many other mammals.
source: In support of this analogy, a penile bone (baculum) differentiates from this region in the mouse as in many other mammals.
evidence: Based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Changes in the regulatory landscape architecture associated with transcriptional activity seem to be a pervasive feature during development.
source: The hereby described changes in the regulatory landscape architecture associated with transcriptional activity seem to be a pervasive feature during development (Andrey et al., 2017; Freire-Pritchett et al., 2017; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When 'active' contacts disappear along with transcription being switched off, the TAD structure comes back to an inactive configuration.
source: We show that when these 'active' contacts disappear along with transcription being switched off, the TAD structure comes back to an inactive configuration.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data analysis.

claim: Negative ground-state structures may simply reflect the absence of upstream factors and/or represent a scaffold to reinforce future enhancer-promoter contacts.
source: While such negative ground-state structures may simply reflect the absence of upstream factors and/or represent a scaffold to reinforce future enhancer-promoter contacts (Paliou et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A rapid return to an inactive chromatin conformation of C-DOM may help control the prevention of ectopic Hoxd13 production.
source: A rapid return to an inactive chromatin conformation of C-DOM may help control this aspect, unlike other contexts where a particular chromatin topology is maintained for a long time (Fernandez-Albert et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on speculation and comparison to other contexts.

claim: HOX13 products are potent dominant negative proteins.
source: HOX13 products are indeed potent dominant negative proteins (Darbellay et al., 2019; Villavicencio-Lorini et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ectopic production of HOX13 proteins in time and space must be prevented for proper development to be achieved.
source: and their ectopic production in time and space must be prevented for proper development to be achieved (e.g. Young et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The deletion of the most centromeric part of C-DOM unexpectedly resulted in a slight but significant upregulation of Hoxd13 expression.
source: The deletion of the most centromeric part of C-DOM unexpectedly resulted in a slight but significant upregulation of Hoxd13 expression.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data from Del(SB-Atf2) allele.

claim: Some sequences in the most centromeric region of C-DOM may contact Hoxd13 and thus prevent it to access more potent enhancers located at more proximal positions.
source: Some sequences in this region may contact Hoxd13 and thus prevent it to access more potent enhancers located at more proximal positions.
evidence: Speculative explanation for upregulation observed in Del(SB-Atf2) allele.

claim: The upregulation effect in Del(SB-Atf2) may be a consequence of a global reorganization of the genomic landscape, as this specific deletion removes a TAD boundary.
source: Also, this effect may be a consequence of a global reorganization of the genomic landscape, for this specific deletion removes a TAD boundary.
evidence: Speculative explanation for upregulation observed in Del(SB-Atf2) allele.

claim: The systematic analysis of single enhancer deletions echoes previous studies where deleting a single and well-characterized enhancer did not have the expected effect upon its target gene.
source: This systematic analysis echoes previous studies where deleting a single and well-characterized enhancer did not have the expected effect upon its target gene (e.g. Cretekos et al., 2008; Frankel et al., 2010; Osterwalder et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The deletion of the Prox enhancer resulted in a decrease in Hoxd13 transcripts, which in itself could account for the decrease observed when the larger rel1 to rel5 DNA fragment was deleted.
source: In contrast, the deletion of the Prox enhancer resulted in a decrease in Hoxd13 transcripts, which in itself could account for the decrease observed when the larger rel1 to rel5 DNA fragment was deleted.
evidence: Based on comparison of RT-qPCR data from Del(Prox) and Del(rel1-rel5) alleles.

claim: Prox seemed to act independently of the other elements in C-DOM, as initially expected for a 'classical' enhancer sequence.
source: Therefore, Prox seemed to act independently of the other elements in C-DOM, as initially expected for a 'classical' enhancer sequence.
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq and 4C-seq data showing no major changes in Del(Prox).

claim: The elements located within the rel5 to SB central part of C-DOM whose deletions in isolation had no detectable effect could be functionally redundant with one another.
source: Concerning the elements located within the rel5 to SB central part of C-DOM whose deletions in isolation had no detectable effect, they could be functionally redundant with one another
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of effect.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms could be implemented to re-direct the lost interactions towards another enhancer when single enhancers are deleted.
source: or, alternatively, compensatory mechanisms could be implemented for instance to re-direct the lost interactions towards another enhancer.
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of effect.

claim: Evolution might have selected regulatory processes to cope when facing particular conditions not necessarily tractable in laboratory conditions.
source: Also, evolution might have selected regulatory processes to cope when facing particular conditions not necessarily tractable in laboratory conditions (Frankel et al., 2010; Hong et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Some functional overlap between enhancers may account for the absence of phenotype when single enhancers are deleted.
source: Therefore, some functional overlap between enhancers may account for the absence of phenotype (Osterwalder et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: It is possible that the experimental approach lacks the resolution required to discern mild alterations in gene expression, perhaps occurring in a subpopulation of cells.
source: Finally, it is possible either that our experimental approach lacks the resolution required to discern mild alterations in gene expression, perhaps occurring in a subpopulation of cells
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of observed effect.

claim: Individual C-DOM enhancers elements may control gene expression at distinct developmental stages.
source: or that individual C-DOM enhancers elements may control gene expression at distinct developmental stages.
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of observed effect.

claim: Phase-separation-induced condensates of RNA Pol II, transcription factors and the Mediator complex are present at particular enhancers leading to transcriptional activation.
source: Besides these potential explanations, the binding of HOX13 proteins to most -if not all- of these C-DOM regulatory sequences raise yet another potential explanation related to recent work showing that phase-separation-induced condensates of RNA Pol II, transcription factors (TF) and the Mediator complex are present at particular enhancers leading to transcriptional activation (Boija et al., 2018; Hnisz et al., 2017; Sabari et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Condensate formation would be beneficial for transcriptional activation and could be promoted by the aggregation of protein containing intrinsically disordered regions.
source: In this view, condensate formation would be beneficial for transcriptional activation and could be promoted by the aggregation of protein containing intrinsically disordered regions (Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Both HOXD13 and HOXA13 contain long stretches of monotonic amino-acids (poly-Ala, Poly-Glu, Poly-Ser).
source: Both HOXD13 and HOXA13 contain long stretches of monotonic amino-acids (poly-Ala, Poly-Glu, Poly-Ser) (Akarsu et al., 1996; Mortlock and Innis, 1997; Muragaki et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HOX13 proteins could contribute to the building of a micro-environment by using the TAD as a scaffold, forming a sort of a super-condensate.
source: which could thus contribute to the building of this micro-environment by using the TAD as a scaffold, forming a sort of a super-condensate.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on protein properties.

claim: Naturally-occurring modifications in the lengths of amino-acid repeats in HOX13 proteins were shown to drastically affect the function of HOX13 proteins.
source: Naturally-occurring modifications in the lengths of these amino-acids repeats were shown to drastically affect the function of HOX13 proteins (Bruneau et al., 2001; Muragaki et al., 1996; Utsch et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effects of amino-acid repeat modifications upon a potential regulatory structure has not yet been evaluated.
source: Yet their effects upon a potential regulatory structure has not yet been evaluated.
evidence: Statement about lack of previous research.

claim: Binding of HOX13 proteins over C-DOM involved most -yet not all- sequences characterized as accessible by ATAC-seq.
source: Binding of HOX13 proteins over C-DOM involved most -yet not all- sequences characterized as accessible by ATAC-seq.
evidence: Based on comparison of CUT and RUN and ATAC-seq data.

claim: In the case of the Prox sequence, a robust association of HOX13 was detected by CUT and RUN before an ATAC-seq peak could be scored, in support of the idea that HOX13 protein may in some instances display a pioneer effect.
source: In the case of the Prox sequence a robust association was detected by CUT and RUN before an ATAC-seq peak could be scored, in support of the idea that HOX13 protein may in some instances display a pioneer effect (Bulajić et al., 2019; Desanlis et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on inference from CUT and RUN and ATAC-seq data, supported by citations.

claim: The Rel5-SB sub-region of C-DOM contains the largest series of defined GT regulatory sequences involved in Hoxd13 regulation.
source: The Rel5-SB sub-region of C-DOM contains the largest series of defined GT regulatory sequences involved in Hoxd13 regulation.
evidence: Based on previous characterization and deletion experiments.

claim: The CTCF site in island V was initially assumed to help increase the spatial proximity between enhancers and Hoxd13 through looping due to the presence of several CTCF sites around Hoxd13 with convergent orientations.
source: We initially assumed that this site could help increasing the spatial proximity between these enhancers and Hoxd13 through looping due to the presence of several CTCF sites around Hoxd13 with convergent orientations (Rodríguez-Carballo et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on initial hypothesis and previous observations.

claim: After inversion of island V and the CTCF site contained within, the effects upon the global chromatin architecture were marginal, consistent with the lack of transcriptional decrease observed upon deleting this element.
source: After inversion of island V and the CTCF site contained within, the effects upon the global chromatin architecture were marginal, consistent with the lack of transcriptional decrease observed upon deleting this element.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq and RT-qPCR data from Inv(V) and Del(V) alleles.

claim: All other identified regulatory sequences located nearby island V were still able to contact Hoxd13 with the same profile after inversion, suggesting that this CTCF site had no major role in securing interactions between these enhancers and Hoxd13.
source: All other identified regulatory sequences located nearby were still able to contact Hoxd13 with the same profile, suggesting that this CTCF site had no major role in securing interactions between these enhancers and Hoxd13, similar to what was suggested at another developmentally regulated locus (Williamson et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on 4C-seq data from Inv(V) allele and comparison to previous study.

claim: The inversion of island V resulted in a slight reallocation of intra-TAD interactions, but they were not sufficient to elicit changes in gene expression and had negligible impact on long-range regulation of Hoxd genes by C-DOM.
source: While the inversion of island V thus resulted in a slight reallocation of intra-TAD interactions, they were not sufficient to elicit changes in gene expression and had negligible impact on long-range regulation of Hoxd genes by C-DOM.
evidence: Based on 4C-seq and RT-qPCR data from Inv(V) allele.

claim: We may be missing the time and/or cellular resolution to observe the impact of removing CTCF sites.
source: Alternatively, we may be missing the time and/or cellular resolution to observe the impact of removing these sites.
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of observed effect.
